proof:
# Strict improvement of a tight simplex row under any small corner truncation

This is a local ordinary-body theorem in every d>=2. It neither proves the joint-row inequality for general bodies nor preserves neighboring mixed fibers.

## 1. Data and an actual admissible truncation

Let K be a d-simplex, with an interior source y and d+1 spanning balanced normals. Each source hyperplane strictly isolates a distinct vertex. Use raw cap volumes Q_l, volume k, normalized sections sigma_l, and

    M=sum_l Q_l/sigma_l,
    f_l=d k^(1/d) Q_l^((d-1)/d)/(sigma_l M).

Suppose the selected row i is tight in the proved simplex joint-row inequality. Put p=d/(d-1) and

    Phi_i(f)=f_i+(d-1)((sum_(l!=i)f_l)/d)^p.

The equality characterization in `candidate bbd1a18ecbb9d3f0` implies

    f_i=x in (0,d),
    f_l=z>0 for every l!=i,
    x+(d-1)z^p=d.

Choose any vertex P_j. Because the cap incidences are strict, a sufficiently small corner at P_j lies in cap j and outside every other cap, and is disjoint from all the source cutting hyperplanes. Cut off that corner by a hyperplane parallel to the opposite simplex facet. This produces an actual convex truncated simplex containing y. Parameterize the lost volume by E>0; all sufficiently small E occur continuously and monotonically. Exactly,

    k(E)=k-E,
    Q_j(E)=Q_j-E,       Q_l(E)=Q_l for l!=j,
    sigma_l(E)=sigma_l for every l,
    M(E)=M-E/sigma_j.

Thus all data are smooth functions of E near zero. This parameterization avoids incorrectly identifying a volume derivative with a displacement derivative, which would vanish at zero in dimensions greater than one.

## 2. Exact derivative formula

Set

    C=x+d z^p=(d^2-x)/(d-1),
    T=d k/(sigma_j M)>0.

The gradient of Phi_i has coordinate 1 at i and z^(1/(d-1)) at every other index. Hence its Euler pairing with f is C. Logarithmic differentiation gives

    f_l'(0)/f_l=-1/(d k)+1/(sigma_j M)
                   -((d-1)/d) 1_(l=j)/Q_j.

Also f_j=T(Q_j/k)^((d-1)/d). It follows that

    d k Phi_i'(0)=-C+C T-(d-1)x^(-1/(d-1)) T^p,
                                                   if j=i;       (1)
    d k Phi_i'(0)=-C+C T-(d-1)T^p,
                                                   if j!=i.      (2)

These expressions use the same actual section and cap data. There is no independent alteration of the other row coordinates.

## 3. Both derivatives are strictly negative

For the selected corner, minimize

    R(T)=C(1-T)+(d-1)x^(-1/(d-1))T^p

over T>0. Its unique minimum is at T=x(C/d)^(d-1), and its value is

    C-x(C/d)^d = C[1-x C^(d-1)/d^d].

This is positive. Indeed x C^(d-1) is strictly increasing for 0<x<d: its logarithmic derivative is 1/x-1/C>0, since C-x=d(d-x)/(d-1)>0. Its value at x=d is d^d. Equation (1) is therefore strictly negative.

For a different corner, the analogous minimum of

    R(T)=C(1-T)+(d-1)T^p

is attained at T=(C/d)^(d-1), and equals

    C-(C/d)^d=C[1-C^(d-1)/d^d].

Here d<C<d^2/(d-1). For r=d-1>=1,

    (1+1/r)^r<=r+1=d,

because each binomial coefficient divided by r to its degree is at most one, and there are r+1 terms. Therefore (C/d)^(d-1)<(d/(d-1))^(d-1)<=d, making the last displayed minimum strictly positive. Equation (2) is strictly negative as well.

Consequently every sufficiently small actual corner truncation makes the selected tight row strict. The assertion applies to every vertex, including a vertex different from the selected row. It concerns that selected row; any other row already strict remains so by continuity. If another row is also tight, the same argument applied to that row proves its strict improvement. Hence all joint-row inequalities hold strictly after every sufficiently small corner truncation of a tight simplex configuration.

For d=2 the two negative derivative certificates are quadratic. At the selected corner, with a=sqrt(k/Q_i), the numerator is

    (4-x)+x a^2-x(4-x)a,

whose discriminant is -x(4-x)(x-2)^2<0. At another corner the numerator is T^2-(4-x)T+(4-x), whose discriminant is -x(4-x)<0. These recover the direct planar formulas.

No finite-large-truncation monotonicity or general shape localization follows from this first-variation theorem. Convexity, source membership and every cutting-section invariance were supplied by the actual small corner construction.
